Load and Calculator inputs 100 monthly active users; 100,000 HTTP API calls (20,000 bounded keyword scans, 77,000 exact policy lookups, 3,000 document/library/status calls). 500 PDF uploads of 2 MiB; 1,000 downloads of 2 MiB. Direct regional internet egress allowance in this model is 2.1 GB including API responses. Upload ingress is free. CloudFront serves the static UI: 20,000 HTTPS requests, 5 GB outbound, modeled at Europe edge prices because the template uses PriceClass_100. Actual edge usage and response sizes change the result. S3-to-CloudFront origin transfer is not counted again as direct internet egress.
Lambda x86: API 100,000 × 0.2 s × 0.125 GB; worker 500 × 1 s × 0.25 GB; scheduled recovery 21,600 × 0.1 s × 0.125 GB. Total 122,100 invocations and 2,895 GB-seconds. Durations are assumptions; replace with CloudWatch measurements after an approved deployment. The legacy EventBridge scheduled rule runs every 2 minutes, not EventBridge Scheduler; no custom events or Scheduler workload is purchased. Its target Lambda execution is included above. See EventBridge pricing and scheduled rule documentation.
DynamoDB on-demand: 1,050,000 read request units and 10,000 write request units including both GSI writes; 0.1 GB base + index storage; PITR on 0.05 GB base data. This is a conservative dataset model, not a benchmark. A 4 KiB eventually consistent item read costs 0.5 RRU; Scan reads data before filtering. Scan pages, growing policy data and library polling can increase consumption substantially. Measure consumed capacity; if search grows, reconsider indexing rather than adding an expensive search service to this demo.
S3: 25 GB document versions plus 0.05 GB frontend = 25.05 GB Standard stock, 1,000 POST/PUT/LIST, 5,000 GET/HEAD including worker reads, validation, origin and downloads. Stock includes retained older versions, not just new monthly uploads. Standard SQS: 300,000 requests, including Lambda idle polling and retry reserve; message payload is below 64 KiB. SNS gross reserve: 100 publishes and 100 emails, only if a student confirms an alert subscription. CloudWatch: 1 GB logs ingested, 1 GB retained, 5 standard alarms, 1 dashboard. Cognito Lite, 100 MAU; no SMS, advanced security or machine-to-machine token service is assumed.
AI/Bedrock/OpenSearch/OCR cost: 0, not implemented. VPC/NAT Gateway/EC2/RDS: 0, not provisioned by this template. The document worker validates bytes and hashes; the product must not be presented as an AI policy reasoning service.
Gross, allowances and limitations The itemized total applies paid marginal list rates to all modeled usage before account-specific allowances, Free Tier, promotional credits and taxes. DynamoDB storage/SNS catalogues have zero-priced initial ranges; their paid marginal rates are deliberately applied to all planning units to expose cost without those allowances. Cognito, CloudFront, Lambda, SQS and CloudWatch may also have applicable allowances. Eligibility, shared account consumption and account plan must be checked in Billing; this document does not assume a zero bill. Support plans, domain registration, optional SMS, dashboard API retrieval outside the small console demo, VAT and exchange-rate charges are excluded. AWS Pricing Calculator has not been created; no estimate/share URL exists. Enter these quantities at AWS Pricing Calculator, save the actual estimate, and attach its URL/export only after it exists. Calculator may automatically apply allowances; preserve both gross and net views.
For sensitivity use the generated 10× scenario, with fixed schedule and alarm/dashboard/SNS baseline. That scenario scales data stock, MAU, calls, downloads and logs together; it is a budget stress model, not a traffic forecast. Free allowances and price-tier transitions are not applied. Largest avoidable drivers are retained S3 versions, scan volume, repeated polling/retries, overly verbose logs, internet downloads and the fixed dashboard/alarm baseline.
Budget, retention and cleanup The configured policy-assistant-account-monthly Budget is 20 USD/month, account-wide, without region/service/tag filters, using UnblendedCost and excluding Credit/Refund. title: Prove It: Agentic Cloud Investigation Series
content:
Event Report: “Prove It: Agentic Cloud Investigation Series” Event Information Organizers: CloudThinker × First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) Schedule: September 5, 12, and 19, 2026 · 09:00–12:00 Location: AWS Office, 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, 2 Hai Trieu Street, Saigon Ward, Ho Chi Minh City Role: Participant and member of Team HCM15 (Tyrex) Format: Three hands-on workshops using read-only AWS and Kubernetes demo environments Event Objectives Learn how to govern an AI Agent before granting it access to a cloud environment. Investigate cloud incidents by testing competing hypotheses and collecting traceable evidence. Practise working with AI Agents under explicit identities, permissions, guardrails, and operating boundaries. Build the ability to defend technical conclusions under time pressure. Produce three portfolio artifacts: Agentic Cloud Review, Incident Report, and Investigation Dossier. Program Principles The program emphasized evidence over confidence. Participants did not provide personal AWS credentials and did not modify infrastructure. The demo environments were read-only: teams could inspect, analyze, investigate, and recommend, but could not execute remediation.
Each session followed the structure LEARN → PRACTICE → SHARE, combining guided concepts, hands-on investigation, and presentation of findings.
Day 01 — GOVERN · Observe Before You Act Saturday, September 5, 2026
Main Activities Examined how the security boundary changes when an AI Agent receives access to a cloud environment. Identified the Agent identity and designed permissions according to the principle of least privilege. Defined operating boundaries and guardrails before granting access. Used a read-only Agent to review an AWS demo account without changing its resources. Recorded observations, risks, and recommended follow-up actions based on evidence. Outcome Understood why Agent governance must be designed before access is enabled. Distinguished read-only observation from permissions that can mutate resources. Practised supervising an Agent instead of automatically accepting its output. Completed the Agentic Cloud Review artifact and developed the Agent Supervisor skill. Reference: Day 01 — GOVERN
Day 02 — INVESTIGATE · From Signal to Root Cause Saturday, September 12, 2026
Main Activities Investigated a cloud environment that had been intentionally misconfigured. Challenged the Agent’s initial answer instead of accepting the first explanation. Developed competing hypotheses and tested them against evidence collected from the environment. Recorded claims, sources, and supporting or contradicting evidence in an Evidence Table. Constructed a Causal Graph connecting the observed symptoms to the underlying cause. Consolidated the investigation into an Incident Report. Outcome Improved the ability to distinguish observations, hypotheses, evidence, and conclusions. Practised rejecting unsupported claims and tracing each conclusion back to its source. Completed the Incident Report artifact and developed the Agentic Incident Investigator skill. Team HCM15 (Tyrex) achieved a score of 93.6/100 for the Day 02 submission. Reference: Day 02 — INVESTIGATE
Day 03 — OPERATE · Prove It Arena Saturday, September 19, 2026
Main Activities Competed in the Prove It Arena as a member of Team HCM15 (Tyrex). Received an unfamiliar cloud environment and performed a rapid initial review. Built an Environment Map covering the main resources, dependencies, access boundaries, and potential risks. Responded to an incident inject under time pressure. Divided responsibilities for Agent operation, competing-hypothesis review, evidence collection, causal analysis, and dossier preparation. Collected evidence with identifiable sources and timestamps, constructed a Causal Graph, and prepared the Investigation Dossier. Defended the team’s conclusions before the judging panel in the Final Defence. Outcome Applied the complete investigation workflow: rapid review, hypothesis development, evidence collection, causal reasoning, decision, and defence. Completed the Investigation Dossier artifact and practised the Agentic Cloud Operator skill. The Day 03 result was below the team’s expectations, revealing areas to improve in role assignment, time management, evidence verification, and technical defence. Reference: Day 03 — Prove It Arena
Arena Evaluation Rubric Agent governance and operating boundaries: 15 points Environment review and risk prioritization: 20 points Incident investigation and causal reasoning: 30 points Decision and remediation quality: 20 points Evidence defence and communication: 15 points Each hint incurred a two-point deduction, and claims without a traceable source received no credit. A conclusion of insufficient evidence could still receive credit when defended appropriately.
Overall Series Results Completed all three stages: GOVERN, INVESTIGATE, and OPERATE. Produced the three portfolio artifacts: Agentic Cloud Review, Incident Report, and Investigation Dossier. Developed the Agent Supervisor, Agentic Incident Investigator, and Agentic Cloud Operator skills. Based on the team’s combined performance across the three days, Team HCM15 (Tyrex) received the award “Most Impressive Submission from Ho Chi Minh City.” Key Takeaways An AI Agent must operate within a clearly defined identity, permission scope, and set of guardrails. The Agent’s first answer is a hypothesis, not a verified conclusion. Every important claim should be traceable to evidence and its source. Competing hypotheses reduce confirmation bias during incident investigation. Effective teamwork requires explicit roles for Agent operation, evidence recording, opposing hypotheses, causal analysis, and report preparation. A technically reasonable conclusion is not enough unless the team can communicate and defend it clearly. Event Experience The series provided a practical view of how AI Agents can support cloud operations without replacing human judgement. The most valuable lesson was to treat confidence as insufficient and require evidence before accepting a conclusion. Working with Team HCM15 (Tyrex) also highlighted the importance of role clarity, time management, and communication during an investigation.
Although the Day 03 performance did not meet the team’s expectations, the experience exposed concrete weaknesses that can be improved in future incident-response exercises. Completing the full series helped connect cloud governance, investigation, and operations into one evidence-driven workflow.

title: Event 2
content:
Report: “AWS FCAJ Agent Forge - Deep Dive Day 2” Purpose of the Event Overview of Agent Core Core components of an Agent: Memory, Observability, Evaluation, Policy & Security, Tools & Capability Supporting services such as Browser (web browsing/search), Code Interpreter (code execution environment), and Payment (payment integration) Hands-on Lab practice Speaker List Nghia Tran – Core components of an Agent Anh Pham – Hands-on Lab Key Highlights AI Agent Knowledge How context window sizing works, and Agent Core memory: understanding the context window limits of models (e.g., Claude can go up to 1 million tokens) to see why Memory is essential for storing and personalizing the user experience. Storage and retrieval mechanisms of Short-term & Long-term memory: Short-term memory stores raw messages synchronously to keep conversations coherent, while Long-term memory asynchronously extracts important information to store as vectors, using 4 main strategies: Summary, User Preference, Semantic, and Episodic. Memory partitioning via Namespace and access-control security: Using a Namespace structure (folder-like) to partition data for faster search and token savings. Security is established through IAM policies and fine-grained access-scoping mechanisms between agents. Pillars of Monitoring and Evaluation for Agentic AI Systems Observability: Operates on the philosophy “You cannot fix what you cannot see.” Integrates OpenTelemetry to collect data across 3 pillars: Logs (errors/system state), Traces (conversation flow), and Metrics (latency, token cost). Evaluation: Helps detect hallucinations and faulty reasoning that lead to incorrect tool calls. Provides 13 built-in evaluators running either On-demand (during development) or Online (real-time in production). Powerful Supporting Services (Capabilities) Cedar Policy & Security: Controls Agent behavior using the Cedar policy language (e.g., setting rules to auto-approve refunds under $100). Supports human-in-the-loop approval when thresholds are exceeded. Browser & Code Interpreter (Sandbox): Creates a safe simulated environment for the Agent to automatically browse the web/search for information and write/test code without affecting the user’s real system. Payment & Registry: Direct payment integration via Stripe/Coinbase. Sets up a Registry to register and reuse tools/APIs across departments within an organization. Agent Harness & Knowledge Base: Quickly bootstraps a minimal agent with just a model, system prompt, and tools. Connects RAG to an organization’s internal data (S3, SharePoint, OneDrive). Key Takeaways Design Thinking System Engineering mindset: Realizing that when building an AI Agent for a real enterprise, the core AI technology accounts for only 6%, while the remaining 93% is software engineering — memory handling, tool integration, monitoring, and security. Personalization & Responsibility: The importance of personalizing the user experience through long-term memory, while complying with sensitive customer data security rules and using AI responsibly. Technical Architecture Combining Memory sensibly: To optimize cost and avoid overflowing the context window, one needs to skillfully combine partial retrieval of short-term memory with key insights from long-term memory. Monitoring via AI Judge: Understanding how a mechanism that uses another intelligent AI model as a “referee” (LLM Judge) operates to evaluate each of the Agent’s reasoning steps against industry standards. Applications to My Work Applying Bedrock Agent Core Memory: Implementing a chat-history storage mechanism for the current project with retention configuration (e.g., keeping data for 7 days), partitioning customer data by Namespace to optimize token cost and improve search accuracy. Integrating AWS CloudWatch / Observability: Setting up monitoring metrics for latency and token consumption cost of each model to promptly adjust the system prompt. Experimenting with the Nova Micro model: Configuring simple tasks to switch from Claude to AWS’s new-generation Amazon Nova Micro model line to increase response speed and save on testing budget. Setting up a secure sandbox: Experimenting with integrating a simulated Code Interpreter to let the Agent automatically perform complex calculations or data analysis in isolation. Event Experience Attending the “AWS FCAJ Agent Forge - Deep Dive Day 2” workshop was a very rewarding experience, providing an extremely large amount of knowledge at an advanced level (L300 - Advanced). The speakers’ theoretical lectures helped the audience easily visualize how the system operates under the hood before the Agent Core tools automate and simplify it.
Learning from Highly Skilled Speakers The speakers from AWS shared their experience using the Kiro IDE with its file-steering mechanism to guide context, using UV to manage environments, and deploying AWS resources directly via the Agent Core CLI / CDK. Hands-on Technical Experience Explored the modular architecture of Amazon Bedrock Agent Core, which helped visualize how an Agentic AI system is decomposed into independent services for easier scaling and management. Learned how to set up and operate a multi-layer Memory system. Clearly distinguished between Short-term memory, which operates synchronously to maintain conversation flow, and Long-term memory, which operates asynchronously to extract long-term knowledge in vector form. Gained a deeper understanding of the Namespace structure (tree/folder format) used in long-term memory. This mechanism helps isolate the storage space of each actor/session and narrows the scope of similarity search, saving tokens and optimizing cost. Learned the system-monitoring approach through the 3 pillars of Observability (Logs, Traces, Metrics) based on the OpenTelemetry protocol. This helps visually measure latency, cost, and token consumption of each model. Applying Modern Tools Got hands-on with the AI-assisted code editor Kiro IDE, learning about the steering-document mechanism to quickly and accurately guide project context. Practiced using UV to manage and install dependencies in an isolated environment, along with Agent Core CLI and CDK to automate the packaging process and deploy resources to AWS via CloudFormation. Learned how to configure and switch the default model to the new-generation Amazon Nova Micro model line. This significantly increases response speed and maximizes cost savings during testing. Networking and Exchange An opportunity to connect and learn directly within the First Cloud and AI (FCAJ) community, gaining access to real-world deployment scenarios shared by experienced AWS Solution Architects in Vietnam. Gained a valuable real-world perspective from experts: in a real enterprise-grade Agentic AI system, the core AI technology accounts for only 6%, while the remaining 93% belongs to software engineering — memory handling, tool integration, monitoring, and security. Lessons Learned Building an AI Agent for an enterprise requires a rigorous multi-layered security mindset through detailed Access Scoping policies and the Cedar Policy language, in order to prevent sensitive data leakage between Agents. The Agent capability verification process (Evaluation), using 13 built-in evaluators split across 3 levels (Session, Trace, Span) combined with the LLM Judge mechanism, is a core solution for systematically detecting hallucinations before deploying a system to production. Migrating Agentic AI systems to serverless cloud platforms like Bedrock Agent Core helps organizations achieve high reliability in both Security and Scalability, at a cost optimized for actual usage volume. Photos from the Event Add your photos here Overall, this event provided not only technical knowledge but also helped me shift my mindset on application design, system modernization, and more effective cross-team collaboration.

title: Draft 1 — document ownership beyond JWT
content:
Authentication does not establish document ownership Technical draft based on the current Policy Assistant source and local tests. Not published; publication URL/date pending student action. No claim is made about a historical internship day or live AWS result.
An HTTP API authorizer can reject invalid Cognito JWTs while an application still exposes another user’s document by ID. A document ID is an identifier, not permission. Policy Assistant therefore has two different access models: the policy catalogue is shared among authenticated users, but document metadata and files belong to one owner.
The trusted identity comes from API Gateway authorizer claims sub. The API ignores a caller-supplied owner and chooses the storage key itself. _owned_document requires the stored owner to match. An unknown document and another user’s document both return 404, avoiding disclosure of existence. Legacy records without an owner are denied rather than assigned automatically. The ByOwner library query and cursor validation also bind pagination to the current subject; protecting only the detail route would leave enumeration possible.
The frontend clears personal document state on logout/401. This matters when Alice signs out and Bob uses the same browser. UI hiding is still insufficient: the API must deny Bob when he manually supplies Alice’s known ID. Signed storage URLs are short-lived bearer capabilities; possession permits use until expiry, so screenshots and logs must never retain them. S3 does not independently validate Cognito JWTs on these requests.
The meaningful evidence is the owner-negative tests in tests/unit/test_documents.py plus tests/frontend/local.e2e.cjs: Alice uploads/downloads, Bob sees his empty library and receives 404 for Alice’s ID. These use real application handlers with moto/local fake identity. They do not validate Cognito signature handling or the deployed IAM/CORS configuration. After an authorized deployment the student must repeat all protected document endpoints using two actual Cognito accounts, missing/expired/invalid JWTs and tampered cursors.
The design avoids granting browsers general S3 credentials and distinguishes the IAM service role from end-user ownership. Remaining limits include shareable temporary capabilities and administrator onboarding. See HTTP API JWT authorizers for the gateway contract and the Workshop for the complete acceptance matrix. Student review: explain where the trusted identity originates, why 404 is used, and why CORS alone provides no ownership protection.

title: Draft 2 — bounded S3 uploads and immutable versions
content:
Enforce the upload boundary before bytes become application data Unpublished technical draft, 2026-10-21. Based on actual source changes and local regressions; real S3 policy enforcement remains pending.
The earlier upload session returned a presigned PUT. Submit checked size and MIME after the object had already reached S3. This left a cost/storage boundary open: an oversized object could be rejected by the application yet still occupy storage. Client-side size checks do not protect against a modified client.
The revised session uses generate_presigned_post, with server-selected bucket/key, exact Content-Type: application/pdf, success status 201, expiry 300 seconds and content-length-range from 5 bytes to 10 MiB. The frontend appends returned fields to FormData, appends the file last, and lets the browser generate the multipart boundary. It does not forward a Cognito Authorization header to S3. The signature/fields are temporary credentials and must not appear in report evidence.
Submit still validates the stored object. A signed MIME label is not proof that bytes are a PDF; the worker verifies the header/size. This is intentionally limited verification, not full parsing or malware detection. Submission freezes S3 version ID and an attempt ID. Reusing a valid upload capability can create a new current version, but cannot change the version already submitted. Download also signs that exact version, allowing the browser to compare original, worker and downloaded SHA-256.
Tests decode the generated POST policy to assert exact key/MIME and byte-range conditions. A frontend regression checks that all fields precede file and neither credentials nor manual multipart headers are forwarded. The local browser exercises FormData against the actual backend handlers and a simulated storage adapter, then compares downloaded bytes. Moto/local checks validate the request contract and application behavior; only a real S3 test proves AWS rejects oversized, expired or altered policies. Such a live test must use a bounded synthetic payload after account-owner approval.
One operational consequence is deployment coordination: backend protocol, S3 POST CORS and cached frontend must change together. Old cached PUT clients need refresh or coordinated rollback. Version retention also affects cost: current expiry creates delete markers, and older versions can remain after that. See S3 POST policy conditions and the Workshop COST assumptions. Student review: explain where validation occurs, what overwriting means with versioning, and what processed does not guarantee.

title: Draft 3 — honest SQS failure handling
content:
A successful Lambda invocation can contain a failed message Unpublished draft grounded in Policy Assistant worker changes and local tests, 2026-10-21. No claim of a live DLQ exercise.
With SQS Standard, a worker must handle duplicates and transient failures. Catching an exception and returning normally can cause an unsuccessful message to be acknowledged. Throwing for an entire batch instead retries healthy records too. Policy Assistant now processes each record independently and returns failed message IDs in batchItemFailures; the SAM event mapping explicitly enables ReportBatchItemFailures.
Permanent invalid PDF is deliberately marked failed and acknowledged because retrying the same immutable bytes will not fix input. A transient storage/database exception instead returns a batch failure. At the third receive, metadata is best-effort marked PROCESSING_FAILED and the message still fails for DLQ redrive. If that failed state is seen again for the same attempt, the worker must not silently acknowledge it. Missing message IDs are treated as an invalid event rather than inventing an identifier.
Idempotency uses both document state and submission attempt. Duplicate processed records are harmless; stale messages from a prior attempt cannot update a later retry. Conditional terminal writes enforce this even when worker and owner retry race. S3 version pinning ensures retry checks the same bytes. Metadata update and queue send are separate operations; a scheduled recovery function queries due pending records and resends the same attempt. It reduces the crash gap but does not make those writes atomic.
Regression tests include a mixed batch containing one failing and one healthy record, returned failure identifiers, terminal failure behavior, duplicates/stale attempts and frozen versions. Moto verifies local state transitions; it does not demonstrate AWS visibility timeout, receive counts, event-source deletion or DLQ redrive. Current IaC uses BatchSize 1, visibility 180 seconds, worker timeout 30 seconds and maxReceiveCount 3. Mixed-batch support protects future batching changes without requiring one now.
Monitoring must match this protocol: Lambda can return a successful invocation with partial failures, so Errors alone is insufficient. The dashboard includes SQS age/backlog/inflight/DLQ alongside worker/recovery counters; safe logs identify the error class without raw SDK messages. Operators must repair the cause before a controlled retry/redrive, not blindly purge. See AWS Lambda partial-batch handling. Student defense: distinguish permanent input failure, transient service failure, duplicate delivery and failed-state recording during a database outage.

title: AWS Policy Assistant — AI Pilot Acceptance
content:
Objective and architecture Complete a bounded policy-answer pilot on AWS TEST. This is a dated project milestone, not a claim that internship week 26 or the entire internship is complete. Statements use retained evidence, not a fresh service-health check.
CloudFront serves a private S3 frontend. Cognito provides the session; API Gateway validates JWTs before Lambda. DynamoDB stores policies, owner-isolated document metadata and the AI quota/idempotency ledger. Presigned S3 uploads, SQS, a worker, DLQ and scheduled recovery support PDF byte/header/size/hash verification. This is not OCR, malware scanning or extracting uploaded policy text for AI.
AI follows Cognito → API Gateway → dedicated AI Lambda → Bedrock Nova Lite Converse → server validation → displayed answer/citation. The model is apac.amazon.nova-lite-v1:0, using the APAC profile from Singapore. Approved sample data may be processed in Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, Seoul, Osaka or Mumbai. Credentials, user identifiers and private PDFs are not sent to the model.
Lookup/search, owned upload/status/download and the document library are implemented. Owner observations confirmed the refund-policy lookup, one refund-keyword match, three documents and preserved library statuses on refresh. Final AI acceptance did not repeat document uploads. The AI panel has one fixed question, no free-text input and no automatic inference on page load.
Project timeline Date Milestone Evidence 24 October 2026 TEST AI infrastructure deployed with feature OFF; application acceptance continued separately Saved deployment/read-only evidence; successful deployment was not full acceptance 25 October 2026 Restricted AI-ON backend: Bedrock policy added and AI Lambda environment updated Saved deployment/configuration checks; simulation alone was not inference proof 25 October 2026 One owner-operated TestA API acceptance Response/citation PASS_BY_OWNER with bounded AWS runtime audit PASS 25 October 2026 Four-file frontend release, configuration last, integrity/cache/CSP checks Saved release/static evidence 25 October 2026 Owner visibility and screenshot-derived live answer/source observations after one UI click LIVE_UI_ACCEPTANCE_PASS_BY_OWNER, offline source/hash comparison and bounded AWS audit Before activation acceptance Synthetic CloudWatch alarm action → SNS → Gmail END_TO_END_DELIVERY_PASS_BY_OWNER with successful AWS action history; not repeated TestA and TestB are role labels, not login identifiers. Scope remains TestA-only, POL-001 and one fixed synthetic refund-period question. TestB is not authorized for AI and did not see the panel in owner observations.
Runtime evidence The displayed answer correctly gave a 30-day period from purchase for defective, damaged or not-as-described products. The source was POL-001, /policies/POL-001, with the approved hash. The owner-transcribed answer matched the exact approved source excerpt/hash offline; this does not validate arbitrary refund advice.
The API/helper request and native UI click were distinct admissions. Each bounded window contained one application ModelAttempts and usage of 588 input /85 output tokens. Actual Errors/Fallbacks/QuotaDenied datapoints were zero in those windows. The two-request total, 1176/170, is not an account-wide total. The first admission had one idempotency record and five counters at one; the UI admission added its own record/minute counters and increased shared day/month counters to two. No markers or ledger were reset.
Limits, exceptions and lessons Atomic user/global limits are 2/minute and 5/day; the global limit is 100/month, using UTC buckets. Reservations remain after timeout. No retry, fallback or streaming. Body <=2048 bytes; system <=512; messages <=512; tool configuration <=768; output <=200 tokens. CountTokens has not been proven operational. Byte caps and post-response usage checks do not guarantee <=6000 actual input tokens before inference; the owner approved this pilot-specific bounded-input policy. Forced submit_policy_answer input is checked for schema, policy, exact quote, answer evidence and usage before the server creates a citation. No external tool or tool result is executed. UUID → Lambda remains INFERRED, provider request ID UNKNOWN. This is bounded audit, not full distributed tracing. Screenshot contents were owner-provided; the original image was not independently inspected in the final reconciliation. TestB batch-control remains FAIL; the original TestB procedure remains INCONCLUSIVE. The owner accepted denial security evidence with a documented exception, not retroactive authorization. No rerun erased the deviation. The native UI click was clarified later and preceded separate UI-click execution approval in the recorded workflow. Functional acceptance does not erase this procedural deviation. OFF recovery is prepared conditionally but live rollback is NOT TESTED. It does not cancel in-flight work; frontend hiding is not a backend kill switch. The monthly USD 20 budget alert is not a hard spending cap. Model and infrastructure costs are separate; billing and notifications may lag. HTTP 200 is insufficient without output/evidence/citation validation. IAM simulation is not runtime authorization; missing metrics are not zero failures. Releases need pinned bytes/hashes and a verified rollback baseline. One-shot/session/batch controls also require provenance.
Next steps Complete handover and retain sanitized evidence before log expiry. Keep the narrow pilot. New requests, additional users/policies, free-text input, durable tracing and production rollout need separate review/approval. Do not publish credentials, private identifiers, raw logs or internal paths, or replay old helpers.
Project repository. The deployed pilot includes local integration not yet published to main; documentation publication alone does not make deployment reproducible from that branch. This is not production certification.
